claims.text: Rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 has a mixed microstructure containing amorphous regions and primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
Several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases form during solidification of the alloy.
A short isothermal hold at approximately 0.85–0.9 Tg immediately after rapid quenching is the proposed intervention.
Rapid quenching can partially bypass crystallization and retain some amorphous structure in this alloy.
Keeping the pulse below Tg avoids triggering crystallization.
The sub-Tg thermal pulse promotes atomic-scale structural relaxation.
The thermal pulse reduces internal stresses.
The thermal pulse eliminates excess free volume.
Reducing internal stress and excess free volume decreases the number or effectiveness of heterogeneous nucleation sites.
Atomic mobility below Tg is sufficient to relax the local structure without enabling significant diffusion.
Controlled sub-Tg relaxation reduces the free-energy driving force for nucleation of primary crystalline phases.
Reduced nucleation kinetically stabilizes the amorphous matrix.
The sub-Tg pulse will increase the retained amorphous fraction relative to rapid quenching alone.
The sub-Tg pulse will raise the DSC crystallization-onset temperature relative to rapid quenching alone.
The sub-Tg pulse will simplify or delay the crystallization sequence during reheating.
Without the pulse, rapidly cooled material predominantly contains multiple primary crystalline phases.
Without the pulse, the alloy exhibits complex, multistep crystallization upon reheating.
The intervention is expected to work only when the initial cooling regime retains a partial amorphous structure and the pulse is applied promptly within 0.85–0.9 Tg.
